items.title: Shinichi Atobe
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Shinichi Atobe, a Japanese electronic musician from Saitama. We’ve recommended his music afewtimesbefore. He’s been making quality techno/house music, beasting in the underground since the start of the millennium. In a conversation with Tone Glow, he said, “I started making techno when I was 27. At the time, I was working as a security guard. I saved up money to buy a Prophet 600. I was listening to a variety of techno music.” We’re playing his latest album, , which came out in March. It carries on his style of laid back techno, with drums keeping the pace and synths conveying his signature form of energized calm. We’re also playing from 2018, which to our ears is his magnum opus.

Have a fantastic weekend.

items.title: TKB (Guest rec from Ryan Mandelbaum)
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we have a guest recommendation from , a writer and occasional DJ, whose newsletter is a valuable source of thoughtful curation and honest reflections on the world of experimental sound.

Today I’d like to shine a light on an artist who is, in my opinion, one of the most brilliant and overlooked minds currently operating in the world of ambient and experimental adjacent sound, someone I recommend whenever I am given the chance: Timothy K. Brown aka TKB.

Trying to describe TKB’s sound in terms of musical reference points is nearly impossible because, simply put, there is nothing out there quite like it. It is a sound that I’d best describe as elemental – as if he somehow discovered a method for recording the ancient music of the earth itself, the essential and imperceptible melody that vibrates through everyone and everything. TKB’s entire discography is well worth delving into, but his three most recent releases (each respectively finding their way to the very top of my year end lists) are all perfect launching points.

is an otherworldly and at times disorienting listen filled with some of the most unique textures I’ve ever heard. Jon Hassell, Zoviet France, and even the work of James Ferraro and Spencer Clarke are the closest comparisons I can think of, but again… TKB’s world is entirely his own. released just a few months later on World of Knots, takes a much more rhythmic approach, its exoskeletal rhythmic patterns far removed from any sense human involvement, rather resembling those found in nature – the fluttering of moth wings, the whisper of wind through leaves, the mating call of crickets dancing in and out of phase with each other.

is easily TKB’s most serene work yet. While it might be absent of the jittery and at times anxious sense of constant motion present in much of his work, it is nonetheless defined by the same sense of dark mystery, as if one is peering into the very deepest part of the night, and given access to its most forbidden secrets. Don’t let this description scare you off though – this is possibly the most beautiful album of the year, perfect to drift off to. A much needed corner of serenity in a constantly overstimulating world.

items.title: Across the Horizon Ep. 71: Lara Somogyi
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
On today’s episode of Across the Horizon, host Bob Holmes of the band SUSS is joined by Lara Somogyi. Lara is a harpist and composer who recently released an album on Mercury KX Records. They talk about her new music as well as the playlist of ambient music that she brought to the show, including Ólafur Arnalds, Clarice Jensen, Steve Reich, Koki Nakano, and much more.

For Flow State, we’re listening to two albums by Somogyi, whose music has appeared on many of our mixes and whom we featured last year. First up is the new record, , on which she passes her harp through a medley of effects pedals. She says on the show, “I’ve been listening to a lot of music that shifts time for me, or makes me feel time physically. I started making the record because I was curious about time… I discovered I experience it through sensory markers rather than through numerical markers.” We’re also playing from last year, a collaboration with Joshua Tree-born pianist Jean-Michel Blais. Included in our daily playlist for paying subscribers is her unmissable covers of “Running Up That Hill” and “Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence,” among other selections.

items.title: Flow State Episode 345
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today’s mix opens with a beautiful new track from Isik Kural, followed by new ambient by Maxime Denuc and elijah jamal asani. There are instrumentals by M. Sage and K. Leimer, and then a long new ambient piece by Windy & Carl (who have a new album out). There’s a saxophone-led instrumental by Cole Pulice and then a guitar-led slow burn jam by Time Wharp. We play a couple new low-key techno tracks by Mammo and Shinichi Atobe, followed by one of Patrick Cowley’s reissued HI-NRG pieces. The last two tracks are a triumphant piece by Akusmi and a sample that may be familiar. We hope you enjoy.

items.title: Ryuichi Sakamoto
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we’re listening to Ryuichi Sakamoto, a Japanese composer and pianist from Tokyo. We’ve recommended him a fewtimesbefore. The occasion for today’s rec is last week’s publication of of Sakamoto’s memoir, . The book is a twofer: it’s the English translations (by Sam Bett) of two autobiographical works by Sakamoto, the first from 2009 and the second from 2023, the year he passed away. We’re playing two piano records released around the time of those texts – 2009’s . Sakamoto studied piano intensively in elementary school and recalled being “shocked” by Debussy in junior high:

I was browsing through one of my uncle’s collections of records when I found Debussy’s String Quartet…. I snuck it home with me and played it on the stereo entertainment system, this huge thing built like a piece of furniture and covered up with lace. What I heard next was a total shock to me. This was different from any other music I’d heard before. Nothing like the Bach or Beethoven I liked. The second that I heard it, I was mesmerized. My affinity for Debussy was so strong that it blurred my sense of self. I started thinking of him, despite being dead for ages, as if his life and mine were one and the same. I thought I was the reincarnation of Debussy. It made me question where I lived and why I could speak Japanese. I even practiced the man’s signature, filling multiple notebook pages with

We wish you a great start to your week.

items.title: Patrick Cowley
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Patrick Cowley, an American electronic musician from Buffalo, NY. Born in 1950, he grew up playing the drums in local bands and then moved to San Francisco when he was 21.He was fascinated by newfangled machines called synthesizers and in the City College learned to play Moogs and Buchlas. At clubs and bathhouses he heard Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder, Kraftwerk, Tangerine Dream, andmore. Across the ‘70s he developed his own style of synth-driven dance music, collaborating with the singer Sylvester on several hits. We’re playing two of Cowley’s solo records, which were released after he passed away of AIDS-related illness in 1982. from 2017 collects instrumentals he recorded between 1979 and 1982 primarily for adult film soundtracks. , just released last year, collects ten tracks which in the words of the label are “sultry, psychedelic, sarcastic, and just a bit sleazy.”

Have a wonderful weekend.

items.title: Egberto Gismonti
items.author: Flow State
items.content: Today we’re listening to Egberto Gismonti, a Brazilian composer, guitarist, and pianist from Carmo. Born in 1947, he started studying piano at age six, going on to study at in Paris, where he was drawn especially to Ravel’s voicings. Returning to Brazil,he incorporated choro, a fast-paced and expressive traditional Brazilian style into his work. That meant learning the guitar, and amazingly he became virtuosic at a second instrument. In the 1970s he signed with ECM, the German jazz label, which went on to release about a dozen of his records. from 1979 is, as the title suggests, a collection of solo performances on guitar and piano. from 1986 is a collection of energetic piano performances, showcasing his signature blend of classical rigor and folk expression.
